case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court reversed the termination, holding the mother rebutted the statutory presumption of palpable unfitness by introducing evidence that would justify a finding she is not palpably unfit.
key_cases.relevance: It is the published Minnesota decision explaining how a parent defeats the palpable-unfitness presumption and obtains dismissal of the petition.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the district court erred because J.W. rebutted the statutory presumption of palpable unfitness by introducing evidence that would justify a finding that she is not palpably unfit.

key_cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of R.W.
key_cases.holding: The court held that parental rights may not be terminated on best interests alone without at least one statutory ground, but affirmed the termination because statutory grounds were established by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Where no statutory ground is proven, the petition fails regardless of the court's view of the children's interests.
key_cases.quote: the court of appeals ignored the clear statutory directive that parental rights cannot be terminated in the absence of at least one statutory ground for termination

key_cases.case_name: In re Welfare of Child of M.K.
key_cases.holding: The court held that parents were entitled to withdraw CHIPS admissions that the county obtained by threatening to withhold needed services, because accepting admissions extracted that way was a manifest injustice.
key_cases.relevance: It sets out the manifest-injustice basis on which a CHIPS adjudication may be undone and the admissions withdrawn.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that a threat to act in a manner that is not in a child's best interests constitutes a manifest injustice

key_cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of T.R.
key_cases.holding: The court held that substance or alcohol use alone does not render a parent palpably unfit and that the county's testing-only response did not amount to reasonable efforts, reversing the termination.
key_cases.relevance: It is a published reversal where the record did not support the statutory ground alleged.
key_cases.quote: substance or alcohol use alone does not render a parent palpably unfit

key_cases.holding: Reversing the court of appeals and leaving the trial court's dismissal of the petition in place, the court held the county had not proved palpable unfitness or refusal to comply with parental duties, where it made an admission of culpability the gateway goal of its case plan while itself failing to provide the services and counseling that would have made rehabilitation possible.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court's reinstatement of a trial court's dismissal of a termination petition the county failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.quote: The county's expectations seem especially daunting considering the county's admitted failure to provide services, counseling or assistance to aid Ostlund in coming to grips with her conduct.

state_agency.name: Minnesota Department of Children, Youth, and Families
state_agency.hotline: No statewide hotline. Call the county or Tribal child protection agency where the child lives — the directory link is on dcyf.mn.gov/individuals-and-families/report-abuse

extended_foster_care_age: To age 21 (voluntary; youth must meet one of five eligibility conditions; re-entry to 21 allowed; Minn. Stat. § 260C.451)

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met

timeline_requirements.starts_from: The child's placement out of the home of the parent or guardian from whom the child was removed

Stat. § 260C.204; subd. 1 requires the court to hold the permanency progress hearing no later than six months after the child's placement, and subd. 4(a)(2) lets the court continue the matter no more than six additional months before a hearing under §§ 260C.503 to 260C.521.
